hn-50328487.t: Nurses Sound Alarm as 'Uber for Nursing' Apps Push to Deregulate Healthcare
hn-50328487.s: A new AI Now Institute report warns gig apps like ShiftKey, CareRev, and Clipboard Health are lobbying states to deregulate healthcare, leaving nurses with less pay and fewer protections.
ex: To receive push notifications on iOS, you'll need to install Nurse.org to your home screen first. A new AI Now Institute report published April 21, 2026, warns that gig-work platforms marketed as "Uber for nursing" are aggressively lobbying states to rewrite healthcare staffing rules, a push that could leave nurses with less pay, fewer protections, and less control over their shifts, according to The Guardian. The report, titled Uber for Nursing Part II, identifies apps like Clipboard Health, ShiftKey, CareRev, and IntelyCare as the main players reshaping how hospitals and long-term care facilities fill shifts. According to the report, the ten most prominent gig nursing platforms have raised roughly $1.4 billion in funding, with ShiftKey valued at $2 billion and Clipboard Health at $1.3 billion.

hn-50328488.t: It wasn't AI that flipped Proton's charge
hn-50328488.s: Proton's CEO called a request for security testing "loser thinking". Using AI to write code is fine, but for a privacy company, the guardrails around that code are the product.
ex: I’ve been paying for Proton for many years, and it’s what I recommend when someone asks how to get off Gmail. This week 404 Media published an investigation into how Proton’s leadership is pushing AI inside the company. The detail that made the rounds came from the security Slack channel: an engineer asked for a few days to pentest new code before shipping it, and CEO Andy Yen answered that it was “bullshit and loser thinking”, then told the team to stop lovingly handcrafting code and use AI more. A lot of the reactions treat this as an AI story, as if any AI-written code poisons the well, and I think that misses the point. Engineers using AI to write code is the new norm. It’s fine as long as there are guardrails around it: someone reviews what the model produced, it gets tested, and someone is accountable for what ships. What the reporting describes is a CEO telling an engineer, in front of colleagues, that raising a security concern was “loser thinking”.

hn-50320995.t: Memdoor: A team of 5 Qwen3.8-27B models beats Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard
hn-50320995.s: A lightweight coding and automation agent in one CLI binary. A multi-agent harness. Run locally or over SSH.
ex: On a box reachable by ssh, nothing installed there: Decision model. Jev (TypeSafe) answers a typed question about a turn with a calibrated probability in under half a second. Judged reads: search, file and log reads return what counts. Per-turn toolbox: only the tools the turn needs are sent. Stall detection: a turn that stops making progress ends. 44 paired runs, decisions off and on: 22 of 22 passed each way; a codebase question 54,661 to 14,367 input tokens (−74%); an edit with a test and ten one-file fixes read the same files either way (within ±11%) (docs/features/DECIDE.md). Workflows, the deterministic harness. Say the steps; the coder writes one YAML per step. mario runs the graph. Independent steps run in parallel. A step is done when its check passes. A gate waits for approval with the diff. A failed run resumes at the failed step. Started by hand, from CI or on local cron (docs/features/WORKFLOWS.md). Workflows, not skills: the write-up.

hn-50323088.t: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks
hn-50323088.s: One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based.
ex: One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based. Frameworks are “blazing fast,” tools will “supercharge” your development, the right abstraction will benefit both you and your users (DX and UX all in one!). All of this breathless boasting is usually offered with zero evidence. Alex Russell has called this “frontend’s lost decade”, Baldur Bjarnason has called programming a pop culture, and I’ve tried to counter this trend in my blog with facts and benchmarks (at my best, anyway). For a long time it seemed like our community’s allergy to evidence was driven by the desire for greater DX. In other words, devs just liked the way it felt to type JSX in React, and the arguments promoting React or related tools (“the virtual DOM is fast!”) were largely post-hoc rationalizations to justify those initial gut feelings.

hn-50325253.t: OmniDiff – Opensource, super fast, content aware Git difftool, in Rust
ex: Speed measured on a T14s, Intel Core i7-1370P with 32 GB RAM (see Fast). PDFs have fewer than ten judged test cases (see Accurate). See it in the browser: twenty real code changes, recorded from the command-line tool and compared side by side in Unix diff and in OmniDiff, and content examples: an OpenDocument file, a compiled translation catalog, and pictures, still and animated. Files are diffed based on type. A PDF diagram with one box renamed, and a web font with twenty icons redrawn: This command builds OmniDiff from source, with the dependency versions it was tested with. You need a C compiler on PATH and a Rust toolchain, rustc 1.92 or later. The build compiles every tree-sitter grammar from C. The first cargo install takes a few minutes, because of this and the lto = "fat" release profile. Prebuilt binaries for Linux, macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon), and Windows are attached to every GitHub release.

hn-50314508.t: I rebuilt my old canvas 3D library as a small WebGL 2 library – phoria2
hn-50314508.s: phoria2 is a small, fast JavaScript library for 3D on the web - charts, labelled scenes, dashboards and product viewers, on a WebGL 2 renderer with an API you can learn in an afternoon.
ex: phoria2 is a small, fast JavaScript library for 3D on the web - charts, labelled scenes, dashboards and product viewers, on a WebGL 2 renderer with an API you can learn in an afternoon. Designed for ease-of-use by agents and humans from the ground up! Everything you need PBR materials, instancing, points, lines, labels, picking, shadows, particles and glTF models. Light and quick No runtime dependencies, plain ES modules, and views that only draw when something changes. Tells you what to write Every option is validated, a mistake comes back as an error that details the fix - for you, or your coding agent. Open source MIT licensed. npm install phoria2 , then find the code, the docs and a React example on GitHub . A rewrite of phoria.js , a JavaScript library from 2013 that rendered 3D onto the canvas 2D context. Back when we were still wizards. Copyright © Kevin Roast 2013-2026 · GitHub · npm

hn-50322173.t: Brazilian Court Sanctions Lawyers for Prompt Injection in Court Filing
hn-50322173.s: Two lawyers hid a white-on-white instruction inside a court filing telling the AI to go easy on their case. The court's AI caught it. The fine was $16,000.
ex: A Brazilian labor court censured and fined two lawyers after finding that they intentionally embedded a hidden prompt-injection command in a court filing. The lawyers knew that Brazilian courts (and possibly opposing counsel) used an AI system to review filings. This case may be the first judicial ruling globally to address intentional manipulation of a court’s AI system through prompt injection. The original Portuguese version was posted on X by Vladimir Aras, a Brazilian prosecutor and law professor. Editor’s note: This ruling was translated in DeepL from its original Portuguese to American English. Read the full translation here. The case originated from an employment claim filed with the 3rd Labor Court of Parauapebas in Pará, Brazil. During the judge’s review of the petition via Galileu (a generative AI tool used nationwide by Brazil’s National Justice Council), the system identified text set in white font on a white background, invisible to anyone reading the document normally.

hn-50327650.t: Patrick Stewart taught us what good men do with power
hn-50327650.s: Great leaders, and great nations, need role models like Jean-Luc Picard.
ex: When news breaks, you need to understand what actually matters — and what to do about it. At Vox, our mission to help you make sense of the world has never been more vital. But we can’t do it on our own. We rely on readers like you to fund our journalism. Will you support our work and become a Vox Member today? Great leaders, and great nations, need role models like Jean-Luc Picard. If you buy something from a Vox link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. When Patrick Stewart, who died on Wednesday, first stepped onto the bridge of the Enterprise in 1987 in his defining role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, the Berlin Wall still stood. The Soviet Union would not fall until the fourth season of that show, Star Trek: The Next Generation, had already begun. Yet Picard’s generation of Star Trek franchise anticipated both events, portraying a post-Cold War world just as the Cold War was ending. It was the quintessential show for an age of American hegemony.

hn-50320963.t: An Italian farmer found some unknown seeds in his attic and planted them
hn-50320963.s: When a seven-eared stem emerged from the ground, it seemed like a miracle. What Claudio Grossi had unearthed was an ancient grain that proved to be an answer to some modern problems
ex: Sometime in the early 1990s, Claudio Grossi, a 40-year-old farmer in Parma, in northern Italy, was cleaning his attic when he turned up an old sack full of seeds that he couldn’t identify. The bag, he was sure, had been left by his late great-grandfather, who’d started the farmstead around 1915. Grossi had no idea how long the seeds had been sitting there, deprived of water, soil and sun. Dry and cracked, the kernels looked so old in the palm of his hand that he doubted anything would ever sprout from them. He carried the bag down the stairs, shook the seeds out into a pile of manure and then forgot about them. To his surprise, the seeds soon sprouted a few different types of wheat. One was particularly striking: At six feet high, its plants were about twice as tall as commercial wheat. But the most remarkable feature came when it developed ears—the grain-studded parts at the top of the plant. All of the wheat types Grossi had previously seen grew only one such ear.

hn-50328251.t: Mathematics has changed. Let's act like it
hn-50328251.s: Updates on my research and expository papers, discussion of open problems, and other maths-related topics. By Terence Tao
ex: Updates on my research and expository papers, discussion of open problems, and other maths-related topics. By Terence Tao 1 November, 2026 in guest blog, opinion | Tags: Frank Calegari | by Terence Tao [This is a guest post by Frank Calegari. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] The release by OpenAI on October 6 of over 700 research papers was a watershed in the history of mathematics. AI is now undeniably capable of making groundbreaking contributions across many areas of mathematics. So why are some mathematicians so unhappy? Some of it is the apparent disregard by AI companies for the practice of mathematics. The OpenAI papers — despite some tremendous ideas — are atrociously written and violate our community expectations of attribution. Some of them are even wrong.

hn-50327058.t: Seoul Viosys begins production of rare-earth-free white light emitter
hn-50327058.s: WICOP 3 targeted at AR glasses and AI datacoms applications
ex: Seoul Viosys begins mass production of rare-earth-free white light emitter, with chips as small as 10µm For three decades, white LEDs have depended on rare-earth materials such as yttrium aluminium garnet (YAG) layered onto a blue LED chip (Figure 1). Opto-semiconductor device maker Seoul Viosys Co Ltd (SVC) says that it has now broken that dependence by developing and mass producing a chip that emits white light without rare earths. The chip can be as small as 10µm. Seoul Viosys and its parent company South Korean LED maker Seoul Semiconductor Co Ltd opened up the micro-LED market with WICOP (Wafer Integrated Chip on PCB), which is a chip architecture that eliminates the package altogether. With WICOP, the two companies have already developed and mass produced ultraviolet, blue, green, red and infrared LEDs smaller than 100µm in size. WICOP 3 is the third generation of the technology, extending that capability to white light without rare-earth elements (REEs).
